forecasts.note: Restated at each quarterly return. The Q4 restatement comes from the annual return itself, so it lands on the outturn by construction — the interesting movement is Q1 to Q3.

forecasts.label: Interest payable
forecasts.note: The council's own full-year forecast, restated at each quarterly return.

forecasts.label: Revenue spending (net current expenditure)
forecasts.note: The full-year forecast of net current expenditure — the running cost of services — restated each quarter against the same measure at outturn.

forecasts.label: Capital expenditure
forecasts.note: Total capital spending forecast each quarter (the capital payments return) against the annual capital outturn. Capital spending not met from grants or receipts is what turns into new borrowing, so a forecast running ahead of outturn is a borrowing signal.

in_year.label: Interest payable, as reported each quarter
in_year.note: Per quarter, not cumulative. The quarterly return is a lighter collection than the annual one and sums to roughly 92% of it nationally, so the two are shown apart rather than added together.

news_drafts.headline: Cambridgeshire adults and health directorate forecasts £3.927m underspend at August, 1.5% of its budget
news_drafts.lead:
Cambridgeshire County Council's Adults, Health and Commissioning directorate is forecasting an underspend of £3.927m for 2026-27, equal to 1.5% of its £266.853m net budget, according to the August finance monitoring report (the in-year check of spending against budget) going to the Adults and Health Committee on 15 October. The forecast has grown from an underspend of £3.490m the month before, a movement of £437,000.

The directorate is absorbing pressures in some services. Physical Disabilities is forecast to overspend by £1.1m, there is a £3.1m shortfall on planned savings, and Older People's services are £602,000 short on income. The paper attributes the overall underspend to commissioning efficiencies and underspends elsewhere, and describes the position as "strong" and "controlled". It credits oversight of demand-led budgets and management of inflation risk.

The largest single variance is in the Service Director - Commissioning budget of £3.854m, which is forecast to underspend by £2m, or 52%, up from £1.75m the previous month. The paper says negotiations with providers over 2026-27 inflationary uplifts "are now coming to a conclusion allowing the partial release of the risk budget held back awaiting the outcome of inflation awards". That money had been set aside until the pay rises for care providers were settled, and its partial release feeds into the directorate's overall position.

news_drafts.headline: Cambridgeshire pension fund funding level falls to 132% despite strong investment returns
news_drafts.lead: The Cambridgeshire Pension Fund's formal actuarial valuation showed a funding level—the ratio of assets to liabilities—of 147% at 31 March 2025, but updated monitoring a year later revealed it had fallen to 132%. The drop occurred despite assets growing by £355.2 million to £5.26 billion and investment returns reaching 6.6%, which generated £378.1 million in gains. The fund's annual report attributes the decline to "movements in the Fund's assets and liabilities" but does not specify the cause. The shift suggests that pension liabilities grew faster than assets during the year, even as the fund achieved positive investment performance. The fund, which administered 102,596 pension records across 185 employers, maintained strong employer contribution collection with 99.6% of the £171.5 million in annual contributions received on time.
news_drafts.paper_title: Cambridgeshire Pension Fund Annual Report for the Year Ended 31 March 2026

findings.headline: Multiple public health services under commissioning transition with delivery impact
findings.detail: Behaviour change (smoking cessation) service recommissioning led to recruitment of vacant posts during Q1. Drug and alcohol treatment service recommissioning commenced 1 April 2026. These transitions are affecting near-term performance across multiple public health indicators.
findings.matters: Commissioning disruptions create service continuity risk and workforce recruitment challenges in contracted services; understanding transitions is material to assessing whether performance recovery timelines are realistic.
findings.figures: Drug and alcohol service recommissioning commenced 1 April 2026; vacant posts affecting behaviour change service
findings.quote: activity affected while the provider continues to recruit to vacant posts and establish new clinics

findings.headline: Children in 20% most deprived areas 15 percentage points behind county development average
findings.detail: New indicator shows 72% of 2.5-year-olds in the most deprived areas of Cambridgeshire achieved a good level of development, compared with 87% of all 2.5-year-olds county-wide. Council working with Healthy Child Programme to increase identification and uptake of 2.5-year reviews in deprived families.
findings.matters: Early development gap in deprived areas identifies concentrated service need and predictor of later inequality; targeted early intervention may require additional investment.
findings.figures: 72% (deprived areas) vs 87% (all county); 15 percentage point gap
findings.quote: In the 2025/26 financial year, 72% of 2.5-year-olds from the 20% most deprived areas of the county were assessed as reaching a good level of development, compared with 87% of the whole Cambridgeshire 2.5-year cohort.

findings.headline: Community-based care for older adults improving and outperforming peer councils
findings.detail: The proportion of adults aged 65+ receiving long-term support in their own home or community settings has increased, with fewer requiring residential or nursing care admission. Cambridgeshire compares favourably to statistical neighbours and England overall on this outcome.
findings.matters: Community-based care costs less than residential care, so strong performance signals cost-efficiency and policy effectiveness.
findings.figures: Positive trend vs prior year; favourable comparator position to statistical neighbours and England
findings.quote: A large proportion of adults aged 65+ are having their long-term support needs met in their own home or another community setting with less people needing admission to residential and nursing care homes.

findings.headline: Care home quality increased to 82.4%, exceeding raised target of 81.5%
findings.detail: The proportion of Cambridgeshire care homes rated good or outstanding by CQC has improved to 82.4% at end of Q1, compared to 81.2% in prior quarters and exceeding the increased target of 81.5%. Includes all care homes in the county, not just council-commissioned.
findings.matters: Better care home quality reduces costly investigations, complaints and service failures.
findings.figures: 82.4% vs 81.5% target vs 81.2% previous three quarters
findings.quote: The percentage of Care Homes rated Good or Outstanding by CQC has increased at the end of Q1 to 82.4 which is above the increased target of 81.5% and the prior three quarters of 81.2%.

findings.headline: NHS Health Checks completed at 60% of eligible population against 67.5% target in Q1 2026/27, with recovery actions beginning to show impact
findings.detail: 5,986 health checks completed in Q1 (just over 60% of eligible population) against a 67.5% target. Performance is recovering following introduction of 2026-27 improvement actions, though Healthy You service remains below full capacity. Further improvement expected as service mobilises.
findings.matters: Recovery trajectory suggests improvement actions are taking effect, but underperformance persists and indicates ongoing service capacity constraints.
findings.figures: 5,986 completions; 60% vs 67.5% target; prior quarters showed concerning reduction
findings.quote: A total of 5,986 Health Checks were completed during the quarter, representing uptake of just over 60% of the eligible population. While this remains below the 67.5% target, the increase provides early evidence that the recovery and improvement actions introduced for 2026/27 are beginning to have an impact.

daily_post.lead: Rising demand creates budget pressure on a non-discretionary statutory service; actual annual costs could exceed baseline if demand continues to increase, requiring council to find additional funding through annual reviews
